newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Lebed talks of peace at NATO's military headquarters.
newsitem.headline: Lebed talks of peace at NATO's military headquarters.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed, taking the international stage for the first time, visited the nerve centre of NATO's military command in southern Belgium on Tuesday.

Lebed, for 20 years a soldier in the Warsaw Pact pitted against NATO and now a possible future president, was received in bright autumnal sunshine outside the two-storey complex by General George Joulwan of the United States, the alliance's top commander in Europe.

The 46-year-old Russian ex-paratroop general walked slowly along an inspection line of soldiers from allied countries ranging from Turkey in the south to Norway in the north, the only NATO country which borders Russia.

Joulwan and the square-shouldered Lebed, who has revelled in the high-level reception received on his first visit to the West, stood smartly to attention by a NATO banner and Russian flag as a military band played the Russian national anthem.

Before moving inside the sprawling complex, where in former days the defeat of the Soviet Union was planned, the two men signed the official visitors book in front of a backdrop of the flags of all 16 NATO allies.
Lebed, dressed in a dark civilian suit but with his military bearing intact, wrote:
"The planet earth needs reason and intelligence and not wars. Let it be so."
Joulwan, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander in Europe (SACEUR), replied with: "Together, we can make it happen".

Throughout his two-day visit, Lebed has studiously avoided the language of past outbursts against the alliance and its plans to expand eastwards, limiting his comments to saying he hoped it would not go ahead for a generation.

He persisted with the moderate line on Tuesday. After meeting the Secretary-General of the Western European Union (WEU) Jose Cutileiro, he said a civilised West would not seek to threaten Russia and dialogue would continue.
"We will find an agreement in a civilised manner," he told reporters.
Lebed, a strong candidate to succeed President Boris Yeltsin if he has to bow out of office due to ill health, will visit the control room for the NATO-led peace mission in Bosnia.
Russia has about 2,000 troops in the 55,000-strong force and a Russian liaison officer occupies an office next to Joulwan in an unprecedented show of post-Cold War cooperation.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana has proposed assigning Russian liaison officers at virtually all levels of the alliance's command structure in order to quell Moscow's fears of NATO expansion.
Solana has said an exchange of officers could form part of a new charter governing all aspects of NATO-Russia relations.

NATO says a new pact with Russia could run in parallel with plans to take in new members from central and eastern Europe, probably starting with Poland, Hungary, and the Czech Republic, but rejects Moscow's attempts to link the two issues.
Before leaving for Mons, Lebed paid a brief courtesy visit on Belgium's Defence Minister Jean-Pol Poncelet.
Asked about a renewed campaign against his Chechnya peace deal, apparently timed to coincide with his absence from the country, Lebed dismissed the criticism as insignificant.
"The dog barks and the caravan passes," he growled in his now-familiar deep voice.
